sub: The Eucharistic celebration of the Roman Rite: its meaning, its parts and how to take part
sec: What the word means

“Mass” comes from the Latin words of dismissal, “Ite, missa est” (“Go, it is the sending”). The name reminds us that the Eucharist ends in mission: we are sent out to live what we have celebrated. The Mass is also called the Eucharist (thanksgiving), the Holy Sacrifice, the Lord's Supper and Holy Communion (CCC 1328–1332).

At every Mass the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross is made present; bread and wine become his Body and Blood; and the faithful are fed with him. It is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (Lumen Gentium 11).
Its roots

The Roman Rite goes back to the liturgy of the Church of Rome. Its oldest Eucharistic Prayer, the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I), was substantially fixed by the sixth century. After the Second Vatican Council the Missal was renewed (1970), and the present English translation dates from 2011; in India the Mass is celebrated in many languages, including Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi and English.

Already in the second century St Justin Martyr described the Sunday celebration: readings from the apostles and prophets, a homily, prayers, the bringing of bread and wine, the great thanksgiving, the “Amen” of the people and Communion (First Apology 65–67). The shape of the Mass is that old.
How it unfolds
1. Introductory Rites. Entrance chant, sign of the Cross and greeting; the Penitential Act; the Kyrie; the Gloria on Sundays (outside Advent and Lent) and feasts; the Collect.

2. Liturgy of the Word. The First Reading (usually from the Old Testament), the Responsorial Psalm, the Second Reading on Sundays, the Gospel Acclamation and the Gospel, the homily, the Creed on Sundays and solemnities, and the Universal Prayer (Prayer of the Faithful).

3. Liturgy of the Eucharist. The preparation of the gifts; the Eucharistic Prayer with its Preface and Sanctus, the Epiclesis over the gifts, the Institution Narrative and Consecration, the Anamnesis (memorial) and offering, the intercessions, and the final Doxology answered by the great “Amen”.

4. Communion Rite and Concluding Rites. The Lord's Prayer, the Sign of Peace, the Lamb of God with the breaking of the bread, Holy Communion, the prayer after Communion; then the blessing and the dismissal: “Go forth, the Mass is ended.”
What the Church believes
The Mass is a true sacrifice, the memorial of Christ's Passover, making present the sacrifice of the Cross (CCC 1362–1367).

By the consecration the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the Body and Blood of Christ: transubstantiation. Christ is present whole and entire under each species and in each part (CCC 1374–1377).
The priest acts in the person of Christ the Head; the whole assembly offers the sacrifice through the priest and with him (CCC 1348, 1368).
The Eucharist makes the Church: it unites us with Christ and with one another, commits us to the poor, and is the pledge of future glory (CCC 1396–1405).
How to take part well
Arrive in time; observe silence before Mass; take part with full, conscious and active participation (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14): listening, responding, singing, and offering yourself with Christ.

Observe the Eucharistic fast of one hour before Communion (water and medicine excepted; Code of Canon Law c. 919). Receive Communion reverently, in the manner approved in your diocese; say “Amen” to “The Body of Christ” as a confession of faith.
The altar and what surrounds it

The altar is the centre of the church: it is both the altar of the sacrifice and the table of the Lord, and it stands for Christ himself (CCC 1182, 1383). It is kissed by the priest at the beginning and end of Mass and often contains relics of the saints. Near it stand the crucifix and candles.

The ambo is the table of the Word, from which the readings are proclaimed. The tabernacle, marked by a burning lamp, keeps the Blessed Sacrament for the sick and for adoration; we genuflect before it. The baptismal font, the presider's chair and the confessional complete the picture: every part of the church speaks of a sacrament.
Vessels, vestments and gestures

The chalice holds the wine and the paten the bread; the ciborium holds the consecrated hosts; the corporal, a square white linen, is spread on the altar under them; the purificator is used to wipe the chalice. All are treated with reverence because of what they hold.

The priest wears the alb (white garment of the baptised), the cincture, the stole (sign of priestly office) and the chasuble in the colour of the day; the deacon wears the stole across the shoulder and the dalmatic. The faithful express their part with their bodies: standing for the Gospel and the prayers, sitting to listen, kneeling or bowing at the consecration according to the norms of their country, striking the breast, offering the sign of peace.
Questions people ask

May I receive Communion in the hand? Communion on the tongue is always permitted; Communion in the hand is permitted where the conference of bishops allows it, provided it is received with reverence and consumed at once. Follow the norms of your diocese.
How often may I receive? Every day if you are properly disposed; a second time on the same day only within a Mass in which you take part (c. 917), and as Viaticum in danger of death.
Why are some words still in Latin or Greek? “Amen”, “Alleluia”, “Hosanna” and “Kyrie eleison” come from the earliest Church; they remind us that we pray with Christians of every age and language.
What is Eucharistic adoration? Prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, exposed or in the tabernacle. It flows from the Mass and leads back to it (CCC 1378–1380).
notes: Anyone conscious of grave sin must not receive Holy Communion without first making a sacramental confession, except for a grave reason when confession is impossible, with an act of perfect contrition and the intention to confess as soon as possible (Code of Canon Law c. 916; CCC 1385).
The faithful are obliged to participate in Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation; deliberately failing to do so without a serious reason is a grave sin (CCC 2181).
The liturgy may not be changed by any priest or group on their own authority (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22; Redemptionis Sacramentum).
Catholics may not receive Communion in non-Catholic celebrations except in the cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
Show reverence to the Blessed Sacrament: genuflect before the tabernacle, dress modestly, keep silence in church.
Reverence for the Blessed Sacrament is shown by genuflecting before the tabernacle, keeping silence in the church and dressing with dignity.
refs: General Instruction of the Roman Missal

sub: Advent, Christmas, Lent, the Triduum, Easter and Ordinary Time: how the Roman Rite unfolds the mystery of Christ
sec: The year of the Lord

In the Roman Rite the liturgical year begins with the First Sunday of Advent and ends with the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe. Within one year the Church celebrates the whole mystery of Christ: his coming, birth and manifestation, his public life, his Passion, death and Resurrection, his Ascension, the gift of the Spirit and the hope of his return in glory (CCC 1163–1171; General Norms for the Liturgical Year 1, 17).

The year does not merely recall past events. In each celebration the saving deeds of Christ are made present, so that the faithful may lay hold of them and be filled with saving grace (Sacrosanctum Concilium 102).
Sunday and the Easter Triduum

Sunday is the primordial feast day, the weekly Easter, the day the Lord rose (CCC 2174–2177). Only solemnities and feasts of the Lord may replace the Sunday of Ordinary Time; the Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter yield to no other celebration.

The summit of the whole year is the Easter Triduum: it begins with the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, reaches its centre in the celebration of the Lord's Passion on Good Friday and the Easter Vigil in the holy night, and closes with Evening Prayer of Easter Sunday. These are not three separate feasts but one celebration of the Paschal Mystery.
Advent

Advent has four Sundays and two characters. Until 16 December it turns our eyes to Christ's second coming at the end of time; from 17 to 24 December it prepares directly for the celebration of his birth, with the great O Antiphons (O Wisdom, O Lord, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Dayspring, O King of the nations, O Emmanuel).

It is a season of joyful and devout expectation, not of penance in the strict sense. The Gloria is omitted so that it may sound new at Christmas. The Third Sunday is Gaudete Sunday (“Rejoice”), when rose vestments may be worn. The figures of Advent are Isaiah, John the Baptist and above all Mary, who waited for the Lord.
Christmas Time

Christmas Time runs from Evening Prayer I of the Nativity (24 December) to the Sunday after Epiphany, the Feast of the Baptism of the Lord. It includes the Octave of Christmas, the Feast of the Holy Family (the Sunday within the Octave, or 30 December), the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God (1 January) and the Epiphany, the manifestation of Christ to the nations.

The Nativity has four Masses: the Vigil, the Mass during the Night, at Dawn and during the Day. In many countries, including India, the Epiphany is celebrated on the Sunday between 2 and 8 January; follow your diocesan calendar.
Lent and Holy Week

Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and lasts until the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday. It has a twofold character: it prepares catechumens for Baptism and calls the faithful to repentance and to the renewal of their baptismal promises at Easter (Sacrosanctum Concilium 109). Its works are prayer, fasting and almsgiving (Matthew 6:1–18). The Gloria and the Alleluia are not sung.

The Fourth Sunday is Laetare Sunday, when rose may be worn. The Fifth Sunday points directly to the Passion. Holy Week begins with Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, with the procession commemorating his entry into Jerusalem and the reading of the Passion. On the morning of Holy Thursday (or another day near it) the bishop celebrates the Chrism Mass with his priests, blessing the holy oils.
Easter Time

The fifty days from Easter Sunday to Pentecost are celebrated in joy as one feast, “one great Sunday” (General Norms 22). The first eight days form the Octave of Easter, each a solemnity; the Second Sunday of Easter is also called Divine Mercy Sunday.

The Ascension of the Lord falls on the fortieth day; in many countries, including India, it is moved to the following Sunday. The season closes with Pentecost, the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Easter candle burns at every liturgy throughout these fifty days and afterwards stands near the font and is lit at Baptisms and funerals.
Ordinary Time

Ordinary Time is not “ordinary” in the sense of dull: the word comes from the numbered (ordinal) weeks. In thirty-three or thirty-four weeks, in two parts (after Christmas Time and after Pentecost), the Church walks with Christ through his public life and teaching.

Within it fall great solemnities: the Most Holy Trinity, the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Assumption of Mary (15 August), All Saints (1 November) and, on the last Sunday, Christ the King. November, with All Souls (2 November), turns our thoughts to the last things.
Colours, ranks and readings

Liturgical colours speak to the eye: violet for Advent and Lent; white (or gold) for Christmas and Easter Time, feasts of the Lord other than his Passion, of Mary, the angels and saints who were not martyrs; red for Palm Sunday, Good Friday, Pentecost, the apostles and martyrs; green for Ordinary Time; rose may be used on Gaudete and Laetare Sundays; black may be used at funerals and on All Souls.

Celebrations are ranked as solemnities, feasts and memorials (obligatory or optional), so that the mysteries of Christ keep the first place. Sunday readings follow a three-year cycle (Year A: Matthew; B: Mark; C: Luke; John in Lent, Easter Time and parts of Year B). Weekday first readings follow a two-year cycle (I in odd years, II in even years). The year that begins on 29 November 2026 is Year B for Sundays and Year I for weekdays.
notes: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence. The law of fasting binds those who have completed their eighteenth year until the beginning of their sixtieth; the law of abstinence from meat binds those who have completed their fourteenth year (Code of Canon Law cc. 1251–1252).

All Fridays of the year and the whole season of Lent are penitential days and times; the conference of bishops determines how Friday penance is kept (cc. 1249–1253). Follow the norms of the Conference of Catholic Bishops of India (CCBI) or of your country.
Every Catholic must receive Holy Communion at least once a year, during Easter Time if possible, and confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042; c. 920, c. 989).

Holy days of obligation are determined for each country by the conference of bishops; in India follow the CCBI calendar and your diocese. On these days, as on Sundays, participation in Mass is a grave duty (c. 1247).
Pastors and parents should form children in a sense of penance even before they are bound by law (c. 1252).
Fasting must never endanger health; the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers and those doing heavy work are excused or should consult a priest (cf. CCC 2043).

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honoured my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 959–991; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 718–736
